client: I've been really struggling since I got laid off from my job at the tech startup last month. The anxiety about money and what's going to happen to my career is just... it's constant, like this background hum that never goes away. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything practical, like it's not going to magically put money in my bank account or get me a new job.
therapist: You're carrying something really heavy right now, and that constant hum of anxiety makes complete sense given the uncertainty you're facing — this is genuinely hard, and I don't want to minimize that. You're right that our conversation won't directly deposit money in your account, but what it *can* do is help loosen the grip that anxiety has on you, which often makes it harder to think clearly and take the steps you want to take. I'm curious — when that background hum gets loudest, what kinds of thoughts tend to be running through your mind about what the future holds?

client: Honestly, the loudest thoughts are usually something like "what if I never find another job as good as that one" and "what if I burn through my savings and end up losing my apartment." It spirals pretty fast from there into this feeling that I made some kind of mistake somewhere, like maybe I wasn't good enough and that's why they let me go, even though I know rationally it was a whole round of layoffs. It's hard to separate the practical fear from this deeper sense that I'm somehow failing at being a functional adult.
therapist: It's really meaningful that you can already see the gap between what you *know* rationally — that this was a company-wide layoff — and what your mind is telling you emotionally, because that gap is actually important to work with. That thought "I wasn't good enough" is sneaking in and attaching itself to an event that had nothing to do with your individual worth, and it's doing a lot of damage by blurring together the practical stress with a story about who you are as a person. When you imagine the version of you that *is* "a functional adult," what does that person look like — and is it possible you're holding yourself to a standard that doesn't leave any room for things outside your control?

client: I guess in my head a "functional adult" is someone who always has a plan, who doesn't get rattled by setbacks, who has enough savings and stability that something like this wouldn't even feel like a crisis. And yeah, when you put it that way, I can see that's a pretty impossible standard, especially for something I had zero control over. But even knowing that intellectually doesn't really make the feeling go away, you know? Like I can tell myself "this wasn't your fault" all day and it still feels like it was.
therapist: That gap you're describing — where your head understands something but your gut just won't follow — is one of the most frustrating parts of anxiety, and it doesn't mean you're doing anything wrong or that insight isn't helping. What's happening is that the feeling has its own momentum, built up from repeated thoughts that have been running long before this layoff, so one round of logical reassurance rarely silences it right away. I'm wondering — that image of the "functional adult who never gets rattled," where do you think that standard came from, and whose voice does it sound like when it shows up in your head?

client: Honestly, it probably sounds like my dad's voice more than anyone else's. He was the kind of person who just handled things, never complained, never seemed scared, and I think I internalized this idea that that's just what you're supposed to do when you're a grown-up. I'm a little hesitant to go too deep into the whole "blame your parents" territory though, because I don't want to use that as an excuse or deflect from actually dealing with what's happening right now.
therapist: That instinct to stay accountable and not get lost in the past actually says a lot about your character, and I want to reassure you that noticing where a standard came from isn't about blame — it's about recognizing that you inherited a rulebook that may not have been written *for you or your life*. Your dad's "never get rattled" approach might have worked for him, or honestly, it might have just looked that way from the outside, because kids rarely see the full picture of what their parents are carrying. Given that you're now trying to live by a standard that may have always been more myth than reality, what might it feel like to write even one small rule of your *own* for what handling a setback like this could look like?

client: That's actually a reframe I haven't heard before, the idea that his "never get rattled" thing might have just been what it looked like from the outside, and that lands a little differently than I expected. But I'm struggling with what my own rule would even be, because I've spent so long measuring myself against that standard that I'm not sure I know what a realistic one looks like for me. Like, if I say something like "it's okay to feel scared during a setback," part of me immediately pushes back and says that's just giving myself permission to fall apart.
therapist: That pushback is really worth noticing — your mind is treating "allowing feelings" and "falling apart" as the same thing, but they're actually very different, and that distinction matters enormously. Feeling scared while still sending job applications, still getting out of bed, still having this conversation *is* handling it — it's just a more honest version than the one you inherited. What's one thing you've already done in the past month, however small, that shows you've been functioning even while carrying this fear?

client: I did update my resume and reach out to a few former colleagues about potential leads, even though every time I hit send on one of those messages I felt this wave of dread about what it would mean if they didn't respond. I guess that's something, even if it doesn't feel heroic or like enough. It's weird because when you frame it that way, I can almost see it as evidence against the "falling apart" story, but then my brain immediately wants to minimize it and say "well anyone would do that, that's just basic survival."
therapist: What you just did there is so worth slowing down for — you produced real evidence against the "falling apart" story, and then watched your mind immediately move the goalposts by calling it "just basic survival," which is a really common way anxiety protects its own narrative. But think about it: you felt dread, and you hit send anyway, and that's not nothing — that's actually the definition of courage, doing something hard while scared rather than doing it without fear. I'm curious, if a close friend described doing exactly what you did this past month, would you dismiss it as "just basic survival," or would you see it differently when it's not about you?

client: No, if a friend told me they'd been reaching out to contacts and updating their resume while dealing with that kind of fear and uncertainty, I'd probably think they were doing really well, honestly. It's almost uncomfortable to admit that, because it means I'm holding myself to a completely different standard than I'd hold anyone else. I don't totally know what to do with that realization yet, like I can see the double standard clearly right now, but I'm not confident it's going to stick the next time the anxiety spikes.
therapist: That discomfort you're feeling right now is actually a really healthy sign — it means something is shifting, even if it feels fragile. You're right that one moment of clarity rarely rewires a deeply held pattern overnight, but the goal isn't to make the insight permanent through willpower; it's to keep catching the double standard in action, each time a little sooner. So when the anxiety does spike again, what if you tried using yourself as your own "friend test" in that moment — asking "would I say this to someone I care about?" — just as a small experiment to see what happens?

client: I can see the logic in that, and I'm willing to try it, but I'm a little skeptical about whether I'll actually remember to do it in the moment when the anxiety is really loud. When I'm in the middle of a spike, it's like my rational brain just goes offline and I'm not sure I'll have the presence of mind to stop and ask myself that question. Is there some way to make it more automatic, or is it just something that takes practice before it starts to kick in naturally?
therapist: Your skepticism is completely valid — anxiety really does narrow our thinking in the moment, and expecting yourself to spontaneously remember a new technique mid-spike is a lot to ask of a brain that's already overwhelmed. One thing that can help bridge that gap is creating a small external cue ahead of time, like a note on your phone or even a sticky note somewhere visible, with just the question "would I say this to a friend?" so your rational brain doesn't have to generate it from scratch when it's already offline. Would it feel manageable to set something like that up before your next anxious moment arrives, so the tool is already waiting for you rather than something you have to remember to reach for?

client: A sticky note or phone reminder actually feels more doable than I expected, like that's concrete enough that I can't really argue with it. I think my hesitation is more about whether I'll actually pause long enough to read it when I'm spiraling, because there's a part of me that almost doesn't want to interrupt the anxiety, like it feels necessary or deserved in some way. That's a weird thing to admit, but I think sometimes the anxiety feels like I'm taking the situation seriously enough, and calming down feels like I'm letting my guard down.
therapist: That's not weird at all — it's actually one of the most honest and insightful things you could notice about yourself, and it points to something really important: your mind has formed a belief that anxiety equals responsibility, like the worry itself is doing protective work for you. But there's a difference between *taking something seriously* and *punishing yourself with fear*, and right now your anxiety might be costing you more energy than it's actually giving you in terms of real preparation or action. I'm curious — when you imagine actually pausing and reading that note during a spiral, what feels like it might be lost if the anxiety quieted down a little?

client: I think what feels like it might be lost is the sense that I'm doing something, like the anxiety is at least proof that I'm not being naive or complacent about how serious this situation is. If I calmed down, there's this fear that I might miss something, like I'd stop being vigilant enough and then get blindsided by something worse. It's strange because I can hear how exhausting that sounds even as I say it, but it still feels true somewhere underneath.
therapist: What you've just described is actually a really common but painful trap — your mind has appointed anxiety as your "security guard," convinced that the moment it stands down, something bad will slip through, but a security guard that never sleeps and always assumes the worst eventually starts causing more harm than the threats it's watching for. The exhaustion you're hearing in your own words is real data too — it's worth asking whether this constant vigilance has actually prevented anything, or whether it's mostly just been costly to carry. What do you think being *genuinely prepared* for this situation could look like, if it didn't have to feel like suffering to count?
